title: Router scheduling ignores issue business priority among pending candidates
description:
## Problem

`build_issue_router_plan`'s candidate sort (rust/src/router.rs) orders eligible packages by `candidate_status_priority` first, then `pending_since`. That status priority is a lifecycle-stage value (0 = resuming already-active work, 2 = starting new pending work) from `candidate_status_priority()`, not the issue's own `priority` field (P0/P1/P2). Among candidates that are all simply "pending" (the common case), the sort falls straight through to `pending_since`, i.e. pure FIFO.

## Live reproduction

On 2026-09-23, three packages were simultaneously eligible under the same `class:smart` route:
- kbs-f954ad, priority 0 (P0), pending since 2026-09-19T23:17:11Z
- kbs-fa8c60, priority 1 (P1), pending since 2026-09-19T14:32:03Z
- kbs-daf353, priority 1 (P1), pending since 2026-09-19T14:32:06Z

`kbs router run --once` dispatched kbs-fa8c60 (the oldest pending, P1), not kbs-f954ad (P0). The only way to get the P0 fix actually routed was to manually move the two P1 candidates to Backlog first, defeating the purpose of having a priority field at all.

## Required behavior

Among pending (not-yet-started) candidates, sort by the issue's own `priority` field before falling back to `pending_since`. Active/resuming work should still take precedence over any pending work regardless of priority (that ordering is correct and shouldn't change) — this is specifically about breaking ties among "pending" candidates by business priority instead of pure insertion order.

## Acceptance criteria

- Python and Rust planning both consult issue priority when ordering pending candidates, with `pending_since` as the tiebreak within the same priority.
- Active-work-before-pending-work ordering is unchanged.
- New Gherkin coverage: two pending candidates with the same route/class but different priority; the router selects the higher-priority (lower-numbered) one first regardless of which was queued first.
- Existing pending_since-ordering tests for equal-priority candidates continue to pass unchanged.
